summary.text: Organic chemistry is the study of the structure, properties, and reactions of organic compounds, which are materials containing carbon atoms.
Carbon's valence of four, with single, double, and triple bonds, makes organic compounds structurally diverse and their range of applications enormous.
Organic compounds form the basis of all known life and make up the majority of known chemicals.

items.prompt: In 1828 Friedrich Wöhler made urea, a constituent of urine, from inorganic salts. Why was that important?

options.label: A supposedly organic substance was made without biological starting materials
It proved that urine needs a vital force to form
It showed that inorganic salts are secretly alive
It created the very first synthetic dye

items.explain: It was the first time a substance thought to be organic was synthesized without biological starting materials, an event now generally accepted as disproving vitalism.

items.prompt: The concept of chemical structure was a crucial breakthrough. What did its developers propose about carbon atoms?

options.label: Carbon atoms are always bonded to oxygen
Carbon atoms cannot link to one another
Four-bonded carbon atoms can link to each other into a carbon lattice
Carbon atoms are held together by a vital force

items.explain: Kekulé and Couper suggested that tetravalent carbon atoms could link to each other to form a carbon lattice.

items.prompt: How did a failed attempt to make quinine boost interest in organic chemistry?

options.label: Perkin proved vitalism wrong with the attempt
Perkin accidentally made a dye whose financial success made it widely known
Perkin made quinine from urine instead
Perkin's failed attempt closed the field to students

items.explain: While trying to manufacture quinine, Perkin accidentally produced a dye, and its financial success greatly increased interest in organic chemistry.

items.prompt: Why did plant-sourced indigo production fall sharply between 1897 and 1914?

options.label: Plant indigo was shown to be toxic to wearers
Wöhler's urea synthesis got it outlawed
The crops failed all over the world in those years
Adolf von Baeyer's synthetic methods cut the need for it

items.explain: Production of indigo from plant sources dropped from 19,000 tons in 1897 to 1,000 tons by 1914 thanks to the synthetic methods developed by Adolf von Baeyer.

items.prompt: Why might biochemistry be regarded as essentially a branch of organic chemistry?

options.label: Most compounds in living organisms are carbon compounds
Most living organisms are made of metals
Biochemistry was named before organic chemistry
Both fields were founded by the same person

items.explain: The majority of chemical compounds in biological organisms are carbon compounds, so the association is so close that biochemistry might be regarded as essentially a branch of organic chemistry.

items.prompt: How did the discovery of petroleum affect organic chemistry?

options.label: It showed that oil needs a vital force
It moved the field's focus to inorganic salts
The petrochemical industry it spurred drove the field's growth
It made total synthesis unnecessary

items.explain: The discovery of petroleum and the development of the petrochemical industry spurred the development of organic chemistry, enabling products such as plastics and synthetic rubber.

paragraphs.heading: The chemistry of carbon
paragraphs.text: Organic chemistry studies the structure, properties and reactions of organic compounds and materials, meaning matter that contains carbon atoms. It covers hydrocarbons, which hold only carbon and hydrogen. It also covers carbon-based compounds that contain other elements, especially oxygen, nitrogen, sulfur, phosphorus and the halogens. The field overlaps with neighbours such as organometallic chemistry, the study of compounds with carbon–metal bonds, and with biochemistry, medicinal chemistry, polymer chemistry and materials science.

paragraphs.heading: Why it matters
paragraphs.text: Organic compounds are the basis of all known life, and they make up most of the chemicals known. Carbon has a valence of four and can form single, double and triple bonds, as well as structures where electrons are spread out, or delocalized. These bonding patterns make organic compounds very varied in structure and huge in their range of uses. They lie behind medicines, petrochemicals and farm chemicals, and behind lubricants, solvents, plastics, fuels and explosives.

paragraphs.heading: The end of vital force
paragraphs.text: Before the 1700s, chemists generally believed that compounds from living things carried a vital force that set them apart from inorganic ones. Around 1816 Michel Chevreul studied soaps made from fats and alkalis, and showed that fats could be chemically changed into new compounds without any vital force. In 1828 Friedrich Wöhler made urea, a part of urine, from inorganic salts. It was the first time a substance thought of as organic was made in a lab without biological starting materials. Wöhler himself was cautious, but the event is now generally accepted as disproving vitalism.

paragraphs.heading: Structure and dyes
paragraphs.text: In 1856 William Henry Perkin was trying to make quinine and accidentally produced a dye now called Perkin's mauve. Its financial success greatly raised interest in organic chemistry. In 1858 Friedrich August Kekulé and Archibald Scott Couper each developed the idea of chemical structure on their own. Both proposed that carbon atoms, each able to make four bonds, could link to one another into a framework, and that the patterns of bonding could be worked out by carefully reading chemical reactions.

paragraphs.heading: Medicines and industry
paragraphs.text: The pharmaceutical industry began in the 1890s, when the German company Bayer first made acetylsalicylic acid, better known as aspirin. By 1910 Paul Ehrlich and his group were developing the arsenic-based drug arsphenamine, or Salvarsan, the first effective treatment for syphilis, which started the practice of chemotherapy. Synthetic indigo shows how industry changed. Thanks to synthetic methods developed by Adolf von Baeyer, indigo made from plants dropped to 1,000 tons by 1914, down from 19,000 tons in 1897.

paragraphs.heading: Petroleum and big molecules
paragraphs.text: Early in the 20th century, chemists showed that polymers and enzymes are large organic molecules, and petroleum was shown to come from living things. The discovery of petroleum and the growth of the petrochemical industry pushed organic chemistry forward. Turning petroleum compounds into new types of compounds gave plastics, synthetic rubber, adhesives, and many additives and catalysts. Total synthesis, building a complex organic compound in many steps, has since reached molecules as complex as lysergic acid and vitamin B₁₂.

paragraphs.heading: Close to biochemistry
paragraphs.text: Most compounds in living organisms are carbon compounds, so biochemistry might be seen as, in essence, a branch of organic chemistry. Because organic compounds often come as mixtures, chemists have built ways to check their purity. Chromatography is especially important here, including HPLC and gas chromatography. Traditional ways to separate them include distillation, crystallization, evaporation, magnetic separation and solvent extraction.
